verdict.root_cause: At 05:28:54, roughly two minutes before onset, platform-automation applied an environment update to cartservice setting REDIS_ADDR=redis-cart:6380 — the last in a flapping series of five set/revert cycles on that single variable [tr_e7a4b15c617b]. cartservice's own logs show it dialing redis-cart on port 6380 with TLS off, failing to connect after ~5-25s, throwing an unhandled ApplicationException from RedisCartStore.EnsureRedisConnected inside InitializeAsync at startup, and terminating — a continuous crash-restart loop from 05:32:00 to the end of the window, with normal cart traffic served cleanly at 05:01 before that [tr_7f81c8170fba]. Because the cart store is unreachable, cartservice never comes up; checkoutservice keeps accepting PlaceOrder requests but its downstream completion lines (payment, email, message-write) vanish from ~05:30 onward, so orders hang mid-flight rather than erroring [tr_d9c1cce098ba], which is exactly why frontend and checkoutservice error ratios are *below* baseline rather than spiking [tr_dda2b70d2be2, tr_9476ff6c3708]. The failing mechanism is the configuration value itself: it names a Redis endpoint/port that does not accept the connection, and that wrong value is what breaks every cart-dependent request.
verdict.reasoning: Three independent lines converge on cartservice. (1) Change history: cartservice is the only service in the blast radius with any recorded change; frontend, checkoutservice and productcatalogservice change logs are empty for the queried window [tr_544775c2df43, tr_ea1566d818b7, tr_60c9a1bcb87e]. The cartservice change is a single key, REDIS_ADDR, set to a non-default port two minutes before onset [tr_e7a4b15c617b]. (2) Symptom at the named service: cartservice logs show the exact endpoint from that change (redis-cart:6380) being dialed and failing, with the exception on the startup initialization path, killing the process repeatedly [tr_7f81c8170fba]. Timing matches: healthy at 05:01, crash-looping by 05:32. (3) Propagation shape: the alerting services show no error surge — frontend and checkout error ratios fell to about a third of baseline [tr_dda2b70d2be2, tr_9476ff6c3708] — which would be inconsistent with a hard-failing dependency returning errors, but is exactly what a hang looks like: checkout logs show request-entry lines continuing at steady cadence with all downstream completion lines absent from ~05:30 [tr_d9c1cce098ba]. Requests block on the dead cart dependency and never resolve into either a success or an error span. cartservice emits no calls_total series at all in either window, so it cannot self-report [tr_94c91798b50d], which is why the failure is only visible in its logs. I classify this as bad_config rather than dependency_latency because the wait at checkout is downstream of a value that is itself wrong: cartservice is not slow, it is dead on startup because the address it was told to use does not answer. I classify it as bad_config rather than bad_deploy because no image or code change is recorded — every one of the five changes is an environment mutation [tr_e7a4b15c617b]. The fix is reverting REDIS_ADDR (and stopping the automation loop that keeps re-applying it), not rolling back an artifact.
open_questions: Nobody verified the Redis side: it is not established whether redis-cart is listening on 6379, on 6380, or is down entirely. If the server genuinely moved to 6380 and is unhealthy, the config value would be correct and the fault would be a Redis outage instead.
Why platform-automation flapped REDIS_ADDR five times in ~2.3 hours is unexplained; a naive revert may be re-applied by the same loop within the hour.

Each revert unset the variable rather than restoring an explicit value [tr_e7a4b15c617b], so the compiled-in default cartservice falls back to is unknown — a revert may not land on a known-good endpoint.

No latency series was pulled for any service; the hang hypothesis at checkout rests on log-line absence [tr_d9c1cce098ba] rather than measured p99, and frontend's metrics were aggregate-only with no per-endpoint or per-dependency split [tr_dda2b70d2be2].
checkout's log result was truncated between ~04:32 and ~05:30 [tr_d9c1cce098ba], so onset at checkout is bounded only loosely and earlier error lines cannot be excluded.
Triage crossed 4 unmeasured edges and named 12 affected services; only 4 were dispatched. Impact on the other 8 (and whether any has an independent fault) is unverified.

All change-log queries ran forward from onset rather than backward, so pre-onset changes on frontend, checkoutservice and productcatalogservice remain genuinely unqueried — those services are not fully exonerated, only shown to be change-free after onset.

alternatives.root_cause: The redis-cart instance itself is down or unreachable, and cartservice's connection failures reflect a server-side outage rather than a wrong address.
alternatives.why_not: No one queried Redis directly, so this is not excluded — but the client is dialing a non-default port [tr_7f81c8170fba] that matches a config value applied two minutes before onset [tr_e7a4b15c617b], and cartservice was healthy on the prior configuration state at 05:01. A coincidental server outage landing within two minutes of that specific edit is the less economical explanation.

alternatives.root_cause: checkoutservice is hanging on some dependency other than cart (payment, email, or the message broker), and cartservice's crash loop is a parallel but separate fault.
alternatives.why_not: checkout's logs name no callee and show no error text at all [tr_d9c1cce098ba], so this cannot be affirmatively ruled out by log content. But checkout has zero recorded changes [tr_ea1566d818b7] and its error ratio fell rather than rose [tr_9476ff6c3708], while a known-dead cart dependency on the order path already accounts for the missing completion lines. This requires two unrelated faults starting within minutes of each other.

retrieved:
/ Confirming it: The change record shows the variable and both values. A configuration pointing at an address
that no longer answers usually produces connection errors in the service's own logs with the
address quoted verbatim - the fastest confirmation available, because the wrong value appears

/ Before proposing it: A prior configuration for this service must exist in change history, and the incident's

/ Confirming it: Change history is the first and usually the only query needed: an image reference that changed

proposal.expected_effect: Reverting cartservice's environment to its state prior to the 05:28:54 change removes REDIS_ADDR=redis-cart:6380 and returns the service to the same resolution path it ran under from 04:04:18 to 05:28:54 — the state in which cart-service logs show clean GetCart/AddItem/EmptyCart traffic at 05:01:31–05:01:34 [tr_7f81c8170fba]. Observable within ~2-3 minutes of the recreate: (1) in Loki {service="cart-service"}, the repeating 'wasn't able to connect' / ApplicationException from RedisCartStore.EnsureRedisConnected in InitializeAsync stops appearing and is replaced by request-handling lines, and the ~5-25s crash-restart cycle ends; (2) in Loki {service="checkout-service"}, PlaceOrder entry lines are once again followed within tens of milliseconds by payment / confirmation-email / message-write-offset lines, which have been absent since ~05:30 [tr_d9c1cce098ba]. Note cartservice has no calls_total series at all [tr_94c91798b50d], so confirmation must come from logs, not from a cart error-ratio metric; frontend and checkoutservice error ratios are already below baseline and are not expected to move [tr_dda2b70d2be2, tr_9476ff6c3708].
proposal.if_wrong: cart-service keeps emitting the EnsureRedisConnected ApplicationException and keeps restarting after the recreate. Two distinct falsifiers: (a) the exception persists but now names a different endpoint/port — the compiled-in default is not a working address, so the revert-to-unset landed somewhere unknown rather than known-good, contradicting the inference drawn from the healthy 05:01 window; (b) the exception persists still naming a redis-cart endpoint — redis-cart itself is down or genuinely moved to 6380, making this a Redis outage, not a bad client config, which nobody has verified (the Redis side was never queried). A third failure mode is silent: platform-automation re-applies REDIS_ADDR=redis-cart:6380 within the hour, as it did five times in ~2.3 hours [tr_e7a4b15c617b], and the crash loop returns after a period of health — so the check must be repeated at ~30 and ~60 minutes, not only at 3 minutes.
proposal.risk: If the diagnosis is inverted — redis-cart really did move to 6380 and is merely unhealthy — this revert points cartservice at an endpoint that no longer exists and cements the outage instead of ending it, while destroying the one config record that says where Redis was supposed to be. Even when correct, the revert is a fight with the automation loop that made the change; reverting without disabling or explaining that loop invites a flap, and repeated recreate cycles churn cartservice's container. The revert also unsets rather than sets an explicit value, so the resulting endpoint is implicit and will be harder for the next responder to reason about. Recreating the container discards cartservice's in-process state; carts already in flight during the recreate are lost, though the service is currently crash-looping so little is being served anyway.
proposal.blast_radius: One service is changed, but its callers feel it: frontend and checkoutservice both reach cartservice, and both see connection resets for the seconds the container is recreated. checkoutservice is currently hanging PlaceOrder mid-flight [tr_d9c1cce098ba]; requests in flight at the moment of the recreate will fail rather than hang, which may briefly raise checkoutservice's and frontend's error ratios above their present below-baseline levels — that is a sign of the change landing, not of new breakage. On the dependency side, the reverted value is an address, so the Redis instance behind the compiled-in default sees cart traffic return while redis-cart:6380 sees connection attempts cease. loadgenerator's cart and checkout flows are the traffic source that will show the recovery. The other eight services named by triage were never dispatched and are not expected to observe this at all — but that expectation is unverified.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical severity across multiple user-facing services simultaneously, with checkout following frontend seconds later, is not dismissible and no open incident covers it. The alert pattern alone does not favor a particular cause, so the fault class stays unknown pending evidence.
